ety.text: Latin adhaereōder. Middle English *adheren English adhere From Middle English *adheren (suggested by Middle English adherande (“adhering, adherent”, present participle)), from Latin adhaerēre, adhaesum: ad (“to”) + haerēre (“to stick”). Compare French adhérer.

senses.d: To stick fast or cleave, as a glutinous substance does; to become joined or united.
To be attached or devoted by personal union, in belief, on principle, etc.
To be consistent or coherent; to be in accordance; to agree.

ex: press on the two layers of paste to adhere them together […].
Adhere them onto light shades of coordinating card stock and cut each piece of card stock %n larger than the image on four sides.

grp.label: To hold, be attached, or be devoted
To be consistent or coherent; to be in accordance; to agree

fr:adhérer.gl: to adhere; to stick to (rules, regulations)

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin adhaerēre. Compare the inherited Old French term aerdre, still used in Northern France (see Picard aerde).
From Latin adhaerēre (“to cleave, stick to”).

es:pegarse.gl: to stick, to cling, to adhere

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin adhaerēre, with change of conjugation.
From earlier *sequire, from Vulgar Latin *sequīre of deponent Classical Latin sequī, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sékʷetor, derived from the root *sekʷ- (“follow”).
